A head study from blockout to finish

A head sculpt is usually finished in the wrong order. Detail gets added before the form is actually right, and then the detail has to be destroyed to fix the form. These are the notes from a study built to make that mistake visible early.

Blockout is a decision, not a stage

The blockout is where the sculpt is actually designed. Everything after it is refinement. That sounds obvious, but the temptation is to treat it as a rough sketch that will be corrected later — and a rough sketch that is allowed to be wrong never gets fixed, because the fixes are now buried under detail.

The test is simple: if the silhouette reads at five percent opacity from across the room, the blockout is right. If it needs shading to be legible, the form is not there yet, and no amount of pore detail will rescue it.

The expression lives in three places

An angry expression is not a single gesture. It is the brow, the jaw and the mouth working together, and each one can be wrong while the others are right — which is exactly what makes a face look uncanny.

  • The brow: the inner corners pull down and together. Getting the inner corner right is most of the expression.
  • The jaw: it sets, and the masseter tightens. A jaw that is clenched without the muscle reading looks like a mask.
  • The mouth: it should be the least exaggerated part. Overdoing the mouth is the fastest way to lose a believable face.

Detail is subtraction

The instinct is to add detail until the surface looks finished. The result is usually noise — a surface that is busy everywhere and interesting nowhere. Real skin detail is uneven: it clusters where the surface stretches and thins where it compresses.

That means the useful question at the detail stage is not "where do I add more" but "where do I stop". A few well-placed irregularities read as skin. A uniform layer of them reads as texture.

What the study actually needed

Looking back, the study needed three things: a silhouette that reads without shading, an expression carried by the brow rather than the mouth, and a detail pass that knew when to stop. Everything else — the pore noise, the micro asymmetry, the specular tuning — was decoration on top of those three.

The project

Zbrush Sculpt — Angry Dude is a head study taken from blockout to finish: form first, then the brow and the jaw carrying the expression.
